Import, and do not re-plan: adelic points, reduction theory, the finite volume of the arithmetic quotient and strong approximation from Adelic algebraic groups and arithmetic quotients (AdelicAlgebraicGroups), stages AA.1, AA.3 and AA.4, of which this paper is also a source; lattice-point estimates for convex bodies, equidistribution and the ergodic, mixing and nondivergence machinery from the parent roadmap, Geometry of numbers, quadratic forms and homogeneous arithmetic (GeometryOfNumbersAndQuadraticArithmetic), stage GN.4, and the local–global theory and reduction of binary quadratic forms from GN.2 and GN.3; quadratic orders, their proper invertible ideals, Picard groups, conductors, ring class fields and Artin maps from Heegner-point Euler systems and arithmetic descent (HeegnerPointEulerSystems), stage HE.0, and CM points from HE.1, of which this paper is also a source; orders and Picard groups in a number field from the Tau Ceti roadmap on global number fields, layer 11, and quaternion algebras with their reduced norm and splitting criterion from the Tau Ceti roadmap on quadratic form invariants, layer 2 — both are existing work and are never re-planned; the large sieve, the Selberg sieve and the local densities from Sieve methods, prime gaps and prime patterns (SieveMethodsAndPrimePatterns), stages SV.0 to SV.2, of which this paper is also a source; Dirichlet L-functions with their non-vanishing at one and the density estimates from Analytic number theory, zeta functions and prime distribution (AnalyticNumberTheory), stages AN.1 and AN.3, and the mean values of multiplicative functions from AN.5; and canonical models with the reciprocity formula at special points from Complex Shimura varieties and canonical models (ShimuraVarieties), stage V4, together with the quaternionic curves of Hilbert Modular Varieties And Shimura Curves (HilbertModularVarietiesAndShimuraCurves), stage R18.1, for the statement about Galois orbits. The Einsiedler–Lindenstrauss classification of joinings of higher-rank torus actions, Duke's theorem, and the earlier work of Ellenberg, Michel and Venkatesh and of Einsiedler, Lindenstrauss, Michel and Venkatesh are external inputs and are listed as prerequisites; the roadmap cites them and does not reprove them. Record with every main theorem that the hypotheses are two fixed split primes and the absence of an exceptional Landau–Siegel zero, that the latter is used in exactly one place — the passage from a sum of the ideal-counting function to the class number through L(1, χ_E) — and that the conclusion cannot be strengthened to equidistribution on the whole product, since the joint packets may miss connected components.
routes.reason: GN.4, the last analytic layer of Geometry of numbers, quadratic forms and homogeneous arithmetic, plans lattice-point estimates and equidistribution and says that it will 'separately schedule ergodic/mixing, unipotent-flow and nondivergence proofs needed for Oppenheim/Duke-type arithmetic applications', with Margulis among its sources; its acceptance criterion asks for the acting group, the quotient, the measure and the irrationality assumptions to be named. This paper is exactly a Duke-type arithmetic application pushed one step further: Duke's theorem is the equidistribution of a single packet of CM points, and what is proved here is the equidistribution of the joint packet {(z, σ.z)} in the product, which is the mixing conjecture of Michel and Venkatesh. Everything the paper needs beyond GN.4 is new layers in that direction: toral packets and their discriminants, self-joinings of periodic toral measures, measure rigidity for diagonal actions on adelic quotients, homogeneous Hecke sets and their volumes, the GIT double quotient and the geometric expansion of the pair cross-correlation into relative orbital integrals, and the arithmetic invariants that turn that expansion into a shifted convolution of ideal-counting functions. A search of the layer descriptions finds 'homogeneous dynamics' and 'Duke' only at GN.4 and, through it, at ProbabilisticAndMetricNumberTheory PM.4, and finds no occurrence at all of joinings, measure rigidity, toral packets or the mixing conjecture. The alternative reading is a new roadmap in the automorphic galaxy, since every object lives on the adelic quotient [(G × G)(A)] and the residual spectrum and Hecke correspondences of AdelicAlgebraicGroups are used throughout; a reviewer who prefers that should say so, and the brief transfers unchanged with GN.4 becoming an import rather than a parent. The case for the Part II is that the paper's own subject is the arithmetic of quadratic orders and binary quadratic forms — the ellipse of the final estimate is the reduced norm form of the twisting ideal, and its eccentricity is what the hypothesis of the mixing conjecture controls — which is the parent roadmap's subject.

Section 8 of the paper is a self-contained development in analytic number theory that belongs inside the sieve roadmap rather than in the dynamics. Its main theorem bounds Σ_{(x,y) ∈ E ∩ Z²} f(Q(x,y)) for a non-negative multiplicative function f of class M(A,B,ε), a binary polynomial Q whose non-singular local densities satisfy ρ̃_Q(p^k) ≤ Cp^{k(2−r)}, and a convex domain E whose maximal radius of curvature is controlled by its area — uniformly in all of these, which is what the application needs since the domain is an ellipse whose eccentricity grows. SV.0 plans sieve data and local densities, SV.1 the Brun and Selberg sieves and SV.2 the large sieve with its duality and bilinear decompositions; the route supplies the local densities of a plane curve with their singular correction, the DeMillo–Lipton–Schwartz–Zippel bound, the large sieve applied to the values of a binary form on a convex domain, the extension of the level of distribution, the sieve with a divisibility condition, the decoupling inequality for multiplicative functions, the three averaging lemmas that give the exponential saving, and the variants with fixed congruence conditions. It also carries the local computations of the appendix on points on conics — the Z_p-normal forms of a binary quadratic form including the dyadic case, the densities at regular primes through the Legendre symbol, the densities at the primes dividing the discriminant, and the uniform bound ρ_Q(p^n) ≤ 16p^{3n/2} that is exactly the hypothesis of the sieve theorem with r = 1/2 — and the admissible lattice-point exponents for ellipses, where van der Corput's and Huxley's bounds enter.

HE.0 constructs the quadratic orders O_c = Z + cO_K with their proper invertible ideals, Picard groups, conductor-change maps and the comparison with the idele-class quotients, and derives the ring class fields and Artin maps. Two blocks of this paper belong there. The first is the local and global orders attached to a homogeneous toral set: Λ_v = E(Q_v) ∩ g_vO_vg_v^{-1}, its local form Z_v + 𝔣_vO_{E_v} with its Galois stability, the local and global discriminants, the global order Λ = ∩_{v≠∞}Λ_v, the map from ideles to invertible fractional Λ-ideals, and the different of a local quadratic order with the identity Nr 𝒟_v = D_v. The second is the appendix on principal genus theory: the short exact sequence realising Pic(Λ)/Pic(Λ)² through the adelic norm and the character χ_E, the index formula as a product of local norm indices, the computation of Nr Λ_v^× for a non-maximal order including every dyadic case, the principal genus theorem deciding membership in Pic(Λ)² by finitely many Kronecker characters evaluated at the norm, and the Galois cohomology of the local unit groups that computes the 2-torsion of Pic(Λ). All of this is classical Gauss genus theory for an arbitrary quadratic order, written adelically, and HE.0 is the layer that owns the objects it is about.

AA.4 plans strong approximation for simply connected almost-simple groups with the required noncompact local factor and the level maps and Hecke correspondences built from it; strong approximation is what makes G_res = G(Q)\G(A)/G(A)^+ a finite abelian group and the fibres of π^+ the connected components of the arithmetic quotient. The paper constructs that quotient as a compact abelian group with the continuous surjection from G(A), and proves the statement AA.4 does not: how the pushforwards of a sequence of periodic toral measures to G_res × G_res behave, namely that they converge to the Haar measure on a coset of the diagonal when the splitting fields are all distinct or all equal, and that in general they need not converge. That is the description of which connected components a sequence of toral packets can occupy, and it is what makes the conclusion of the main theorem sharp.
